page.title: tinyactors: like SQLite, but for actors
page.description: tinyactors runs millions of statecharts inside your program, in Node.js, Python, a browser or C: composable state machines that describe a reactive system formally.

hero.headline: Like SQLite, but for actors
hero.lede: tinyactors runs millions of actors as a library in your process, in Node.js, Python, a browser or C, with no separate server. Each actor runs a statechart: a composable state machine that describes a reactive system formally and is easy to verify.

section.heading: Write each actor's behavior as one chart
section.p: A statechart is a composable state machine of states, events and transitions. Because it isolates effects as events, your code can simulate runs in tests.
A tinyactors actor runs a chart instead of arbitrary code like Erlang or Akka, keeping behavior readable and easy to verify.

This payment chart isolates each charge as an event, so your code can simulate the flow without waiting. It retries every 30 seconds in states and transitions until it is paid or has charged three times:

section.heading: Hand a chart to a coding agent
section.p: Statecharts make behavior readable and checkable, but writing every state by hand cost more than most teams would pay. A coding agent does that writing for you, and that changes the trade.
The chart sends an event for every effect, and your code performs it. A simulated clock runs its timeouts, so the agent tests each change in milliseconds.

section.heading: Run millions of actors in your process

item.text: tinyactors is a library on your own event loop, so your actors deploy with your program.

item.term: One chart runs in JavaScript, Python and C
item.text: tinyactors wraps one C core in every language package, so your actors run the same way everywhere.

item.term: Small enough for every part of a system
item.text: An actor takes about 530 bytes in Node.js, and an idle one saved to a database keeps about 120. See the performance page

section.heading: Kill your unit tests
section.p: A unit test checks one run you wrote down. A property is a rule, like "never charge a card more than three times", checked on runs a program generates.
This loop runs the payment a thousand times against a stand-in service that answers 40% of charges. After each run it checks two rules:
With attempts < 4 in the chart, the loop stops at seed 10: it charged the card four times. The whole program is 44 lines.

section.heading: Conquer complexity
section.p: A team chat like Slack looks simple: rooms and messages. Its hard part is the state: who is in which room, and who is online as people come and go.
The tutorial builds one in five steps, and each part of that state lives in an actor:

item.text: Two joins at the same moment can overwrite each other in a shared member list. A room actor handles one event at a time, so its member list keeps every join.
A user who stops being active sends no event, so nothing marks them as away. The user's chart restarts a timer on each activity and marks the user away after 300 seconds.

Most users are idle, and each one's data takes memory as long as it stays loaded. An idle user's actor is saved to a store and loaded again on its next event: a thousand users ran with fifty in memory.

section.heading: Run actors in production
section.p: An actor in production stands for an entity, such as an account, and lives as long as it does. So you change and watch actors that are already running.

item.text: When your rules change, the accounts already running still follow the old ones. Add the chart's new version, and a migration moves each running actor to it, keeping the state it reached.
A snapshot copies every actor of a running process so you can inspect each actor's state. Two million actors make a 165 MB snapshot.
tinyactors traces every step of every actor as OpenTelemetry. You turn it on with an option, not with code.
